analysis.body:
# Grid Interconnection Snapshot for AI Data Center Observers

Across the five major US grid operators, 8,380 generation and storage projects totaling 1.33 million MW await interconnection as of mid-September 2026. This queue represents planned supply side capacity responding to rising electricity demand, which data centers are driving in key regions. Texas leads with 438,086 MW in ERCOT's queue, followed by New York at 319,115 MW and the Midcontinent region at 299,721 MW. Commercial electricity sales—the closest available proxy for data center load—reached 54,798 MWh in June 2026 across eight high-capacity states, with Texas consuming 15,754 MWh at the lowest price at $8.66 per MWh, while California paid the highest rate at $27.33 per MWh for 10,025 MWh.

Storage and natural gas projects in these queues signal grid operators' expectations about future load patterns. ERCOT's queue is dominated by solar (150,347 MW) and battery storage (159,820 MW), together comprising 70 percent of its planned capacity. MISO similarly prioritizes solar (146,004 MW) and storage (67,027 MW). CAISO's queue is 65 percent storage (46,940 MW) relative to its smaller total. This storage emphasis reflects the need to balance high renewable penetration with the continuous, predictable demand profile that data centers create. Gas capacity in the queues—78,092 MW in ERCOT, 47,421 MW in SPP, and 30,236 MW in MISO—provides the dispatchable backstop that renewable-heavy grids require.

Electricity prices vary dramatically by location: Oregon's commercial rate sits at $10.59 per MWh while California's reaches $27.33, a 158 percent spread that directly influences data center siting decisions. Virginia's 7,771 MWh of commercial consumption occurs at $10.99 per MWh, making it competitive for new facilities alongside Texas and Georgia. The interconnection queue depths suggest multi-year lead times for grid connection; MISO alone counts 3,846 active requests, implying constrained study and approval capacity that will affect project timelines regardless of generation hardware availability. Watch for which regions complete their interconnection studies first and whether storage-to-solar ratios in approved projects shift in response to actual data center deployment patterns.
